section.title: The New Tablets and What God Requires
section.sectionRationale: After the golden calf and Moses' renewed intercession, this chapter moves from judgment to fresh grace, new tablets, a renewed priesthood, and Moses' famous summary of what the LORD actually requires, a circumcised heart of love rather than empty ritual.
section.thesis: After Israel's rebellion and Moses' renewed intercession, God provides new tablets and reveals through Moses what He actually requires: fearing Him, walking in His ways, loving Him, serving Him wholeheartedly, and circumcising the heart, since the God of gods who owns the heavens still stoops to love the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: new tablets and the ark; historical notes on Aaron's death and Levi's calling; Moses' intercession succeeds again; what does the LORD require; the LORD of all, yet He chose you; God of gods who loves the foreigner; and the closing call to fear, serve, hold fast, and praise.

verses.text: At that time the LORD said to me, “Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals, come up to Me on the mountain, and make an ark of wood.
And I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke; and you are to place them in the ark.”
So I made an ark of acacia wood, chiseled out two stone tablets like the originals, and went up the mountain with the two tablets in my hands.

And the LORD wrote on the tablets what had been written previously, the Ten Commandments that He had spoken to you on the mountain out of the fire on the day of the assembly. The LORD gave them to me,
and I went back down the mountain and placed the tablets in the ark I had made, as the LORD had commanded me; and there they have remained.

units.label: Historical notes: Aaron's death, Levi's calling

verses.text: The Israelites traveled from Beeroth Bene-jaakan to Moserah, where Aaron died and was buried, and Eleazar his son succeeded him as priest.
From there they traveled to Gudgodah, and from Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land with streams of water.
At that time the LORD set apart the tribe of Levi to carry the ark of the covenant of the LORD, to stand before the LORD to serve Him, and to pronounce blessings in His name, as they do to this day.
That is why Levi has no portion or inheritance among his brothers; the LORD is his inheritance, as the LORD your God promised him.
I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights, like the first time, and that time the LORD again listened to me and agreed not to destroy you.
Then the LORD said to me, “Get up. Continue your journey ahead of the people, that they may enter and possess the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.”

And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to {{yare|fear}} the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul,
and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you this day for your own good?

units.label: The LORD of all, yet He chose you

verses.text: Behold, to the LORD your God belong the heavens, even the highest heavens, and the earth and everything in it.
Yet the LORD has set His affection on your fathers and loved them. And He has chosen you, their descendants after them, above all the peoples, even to this day.
{{mool|Circumcise}} your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more.

units.label: God of gods, who loves the foreigner

verses.text: For the LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe.
He executes justice for the fatherless and widow, and He loves the {{ger|foreigner}}, giving him food and clothing.
So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
You are to fear the LORD your God and serve Him. Hold fast to Him and take your oaths in His name.
He is your praise and He is your God, who has done for you these great and awesome wonders that your eyes have seen.
Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky.

yare.gloss: To fear, revere, stand in awe. Paired here with loving and serving God, it describes reverent submission that flows from love, not terror that avoids relationship; it is the beginning, not the opposite, of wholehearted devotion.

mool.gloss: To circumcise, to cut away the flesh. Applied metaphorically to the heart, it calls for an inward cutting away of stubborn resistance to God, not merely maintaining the outward physical sign of the covenant.

ger.gloss: Foreigner, sojourner, resident alien. Someone living among a people not their own by birth, without full native rights; God's love for the ger and Israel's own history as ger in Egypt ground a repeated command to treat foreigners with justice and love.

basic.context: After the golden calf, Moses receives new stone tablets, and this chapter moves from disaster toward renewed grace, closing with Moses' famous summary of what God actually requires: fearing, loving, and serving Him wholeheartedly, with a heart truly circumcised rather than merely outwardly compliant.
basic.hermeneutics: This is both historical narrative, God graciously restoring the covenant relationship after Israel's worst failure, and timeless summary, since Moses' description of what God requires expresses His unchanging character and expectation for every generation of His people.
basic.originalLanguages: God requires yare, fear that flows from love rather than mere terror, and calls Israel to mool, circumcise, their hearts, an inward cutting away of stubborn resistance rather than only an outward rite. His love and justice extend even to the ger, the foreigner living among them.
basic.typology: The call to circumcise the heart anticipates the New Testament's teaching that true covenant membership is an inward, Spirit-wrought reality, not merely an external sign, fulfilled in the circumcision of Christ that believers receive by faith, Colossians 2:11.
basic.christ: Paul explicitly develops this chapter's logic in Romans 2:28-29, saying true circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not merely the letter, a work only the Spirit of Christ can accomplish, since human effort alone cannot cut away its own stubbornness.
basic.god: God owns the entire universe, needing nothing from anyone, yet He sets His affection specifically on His people, shows perfect justice by accepting no bribe, and personally loves and provides for the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner, revealing that true greatness and true tenderness are not opposites in His character.
basic.crossReferences: Micah 6:8 echoes this chapter's summary of what the LORD requires. Romans 2:28-29 develops the theme of true, inward circumcision of the heart. Colossians 2:11-12 identifies this inward circumcision with union with Christ. James 1:27 echoes the call to care for the fatherless and widow.
basic.oneStory: This chapter defines true religion as a matter of the heart, not empty ritual, an inward circumcision that only God can perform, expressed outwardly in justice and love for the vulnerable. That inward transformation, promised here and impossible by human effort alone, is finally accomplished in Christ through His Spirit.

context.literary:
The first eleven verses finish the story Moses began in 9:7. The breaking of the tablets in 9:17 is answered by their remaking in 10:1-5, and the forty days of pleading in 9:18 and 9:25 are answered by 10:10: 'that time the LORD again listened to me and agreed not to destroy you.' The unit closes where the whole review began, with God's command to go and possess the land, 10:11, echoing 9:1. Judgment is bracketed by promise.

Verses 6 to 9 interrupt the first-person story with a travel note in the third person, naming stations of the journey, Aaron's death, and the setting apart of Levi. The break is deliberate. Right after the calf, where Aaron sinned and the Levites rallied to Moses, Exodus 32:26-29, the text shows that God did not revoke the priesthood. Aaron's line continued in Eleazar, and Levi was given the ark to carry.

Then, at verse 12, the tone turns with 'And now, O Israel.' The phrase marks the move from history to response, as Moses gathers up everything since chapter 5 into one question. The answer is a chain of five infinitives: to fear, to walk, to love, to serve, to keep. Verses 14 to 22 then alternate between who God is and what Israel must therefore do. God owns the highest heavens, yet chose the fathers, so circumcise your hearts, verses 14 to 16. God is God of gods and loves the foreigner, so love the foreigner, verses 17 to 19. God has done great wonders and multiplied you, so fear and serve Him, verses 20 to 22. Every command rests on a statement about God. The call to 'stiffen your necks no more,' verse 16, deliberately picks up the verdict of 9:6 and 9:13 and turns it into a summons to change.
context.historical:
The ark of verse 1 was a chest of acacia wood, the hard wood of the Sinai wilderness also used for the tabernacle's frames and altar. Placing the covenant document inside a sacred container matches a wider ancient practice of depositing treaty texts before the gods of the parties. Israel's covenant was kept 'before the LORD,' in His presence, as a standing witness. Centuries later, when the ark was brought into Solomon's temple, 'there was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb,' 1 Kings 8:9. Deuteronomy's words 'there they have remained,' verse 5, were still true.

The itinerary of verses 6 and 7 differs from the list in Numbers 33:30-33, which runs Moseroth, Bene-jaakan, Hor-haggidgad, Jotbathah, the reverse of Deuteronomy's first two stations. Numbers also places Aaron's death on Mount Hor, Numbers 20:27-28 and 33:38, while Deuteronomy names Moserah. The sites cannot be located with certainty today. Jotbathah, 'a land with streams of water,' verse 7, would have been remembered as a rare place of relief in the wilderness.

The duties given to Levi in verse 8 are three: to carry the ark, to stand before the LORD to minister, and to bless in His name, as in the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:23-27. Because they received no tribal territory, verse 9, their support came through the offerings and tithes of the other tribes, Numbers 18:20-21, which explains why Deuteronomy repeatedly tells Israel not to neglect 'the Levite within your gates.'

The triad of verse 18, fatherless, widow and foreigner, names the three groups in the ancient world with no landholding male to protect them. Justice for them was a mark of a righteous king across the ancient Near East; Moses ascribes it to Israel's God Himself and then requires it of every Israelite. The closing number, seventy, verse 22, recalls Genesis 46:27. The small family that went down to Egypt is now as numerous as the stars, as promised in Genesis 15:5.
context.canonical:
The first half of the chapter feeds the Bible's teaching about the covenant document and the priesthood. The tablets in the ark lie behind the description of the Most Holy Place in Hebrews 9:3-5. Levi's inheritance, 'the LORD is his inheritance,' becomes the confession of individual worshipers: 'The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup,' Psalm 16:5, and 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever,' Psalm 73:26. Peter applies Israel's priestly calling to the whole church, 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9.

The question of verse 12 has a famous echo in Micah 6:6-8, which asks what the worshiper should bring and answers with justice, mercy and a humble walk with God. The scribe in Mark 12:33 reaches the same conclusion: love for God and neighbor is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.' When Jesus resisted the tempter He quoted words found in both Deuteronomy 6:13 and 10:20: 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only,' Matthew 4:10.

The circumcision of the heart becomes a major prophetic and apostolic theme. Leviticus 26:41 hopes that Israel's 'uncircumcised hearts will be humbled.' Deuteronomy itself later promises that 'the LORD your God will circumcise your hearts,' 30:6. Jeremiah calls Judah to 'remove the foreskins of your hearts,' Jeremiah 4:4, and says 'the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart,' Jeremiah 9:26. Stephen accuses his hearers of being 'stiff-necked people with uncircumcised hearts and ears,' Acts 7:51, combining both images of verse 16. Paul says true circumcision is 'a matter of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29, and that believers are 'the circumcision,' Philippians 3:3.

The divine titles and the impartiality of verse 17 are also taken up. 'God of gods' and 'Lord of lords' are sung in Psalm 136:2-3. Jehoshaphat charges his judges that with the LORD 'there is no injustice or partiality or bribery,' 2 Chronicles 19:7. Peter's discovery that 'God does not show favoritism,' Acts 10:34, opens the door to the Gentiles, and Revelation gives the title 'Lord of lords' to the returning Christ, Revelation 19:16.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses has just spent a chapter proving that Israel deserved destruction. Now he wants them to see that God's answer to their rebellion was not to end the covenant but to renew it. The new tablets, the ark, the continuing priesthood and the renewed command to march all say the same thing: the relationship stands. The second generation must know they live on the far side of forgiveness.

From that ground Moses asks his question. He does not load them with a new list of duties. He compresses the whole covenant into a few words about the heart and the life, and he roots each demand in God's character. Fear the God who owns the heavens. Love the foreigner because God loves him and because you were one. Hold fast to Him because He has done great things before your eyes.

The call to circumcise the heart shows that Moses knows where the problem lies. Israel's failure at Horeb was not a lack of information. It was a stiff neck. He wants them to understand that God is after hearts that yield, and that the outward mark they already bore on their bodies was meant to signify exactly that.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Several parts of the chapter record Israel's particular history: the second set of tablets, the building of the ark, the stations of the journey, the death of Aaron, and the appointment of Levi. These are not commands for the church to copy. There is no longer an ark to carry, and the Levitical priesthood has given way to Christ's, Hebrews 7:11-12.

Verses 12 to 22, however, are among the most directly transferable words in the law. The demand to fear, love, walk with and serve God wholeheartedly is repeated by Jesus as the first and greatest commandment, Matthew 22:37-38. The duty to love the foreigner, grounded in Israel's own experience as outsiders, is carried into the New Testament's call to hospitality, Romans 12:13 and Hebrews 13:2, and the church's own identity as people once 'strangers to the covenants,' Ephesians 2:12. Believers who were brought near in Christ have the same reason Israel had to love the outsider: they were outsiders once themselves.

debates.question: How does 'circumcise your heart' in verse 16 relate to the physical rite of circumcision commanded elsewhere in the law?

views.label: It is a metaphorical intensification of an already-required physical sign
views.case: Israel already practiced physical circumcision as the covenant sign, Genesis 17; Moses here is not replacing that command but insisting its outward form must be matched by an inward reality of the heart, or the physical sign becomes hollow.

views.label: It anticipates a deeper transformation the law itself could not produce
views.case: Later texts like Jeremiah 4:4 and 31:33, and Paul's teaching in Romans 2:29, suggest this phrase points toward a work only God's Spirit can accomplish, since Israel's history shows the physical sign alone never produced lasting heart change.

debates.bearing: Both views agree the phrase demands an inward reality beyond mere ritual observance; the difference concerns how directly this verse anticipates the fuller new-covenant transformation later texts describe.

debates.question: Where did Aaron die, and why does the itinerary of verses 6 and 7 differ from Numbers?

views.label: Moserah is the district, Mount Hor the peak within it
views.case: Many harmonize the texts by taking Moserah as the region in which Mount Hor stood, so that Numbers 20:27-28 names the summit and Deuteronomy the surrounding area. The different order of stations may reflect the people passing through the same area more than once during the wilderness years.

views.label: The note preserves a separate travel tradition used for a theological purpose
views.case: Others think the note comes from a distinct source list and was placed here, out of sequence, because its point is not geography. Set immediately after the golden calf, it shows that Aaron's priesthood continued through Eleazar and that Levi was set apart despite the sin at Horeb.

debates.bearing: The sites cannot now be identified with confidence, so certainty is not available. Either way the placement of the note is clearly intentional: grace after the calf reached even the priestly family whose head had made it.

debates.question: Who made the ark: Moses before the second ascent, as verse 3 says, or Bezalel, as Exodus 37:1 records?

views.label: Moses speaks of what was done under his authority
views.case: Ancient speech commonly attributes to a leader what his craftsmen carried out, and Moses is summarizing. On this view 'I made an ark' means the ark was made at his command, and Exodus supplies the craftsman's name and the full description.

views.label: A temporary chest preceded the tabernacle ark
views.case: Some suggest Moses made a simple wooden box to receive the new tablets on the mountain, later replaced or enclosed by the gold-covered ark Bezalel built for the tabernacle. Deuteronomy mentions only acacia wood and no gold or cherubim.

debates.bearing: Neither view affects the point Moses is making. The renewed covenant was given a permanent resting place in God's presence, and the words written on it were God's own, verse 4.

study.originalLanguages:
Moses' question in verse 12 uses sha'al, the ordinary verb for asking or requesting, not a word for exacting payment. 'What does the LORD your God ask of you?' has the tone of a father's appeal. Micah 6:8 uses a different verb, darash, to seek or require, and its answer is tighter still, but the two passages share the same instinct: after all the detail of the law, God's desire can be said in a sentence.

In verse 15 'set His affection' translates chashaq, a word for an attachment that clings, used of Shechem's longing for Dinah in Genesis 34:8 and of God's choice of Israel in Deuteronomy 7:7. It is paired here with ahav, love, and with bachar, choose. The three verbs pile up to say that Israel's election was not a cold decree but a love fixed on them for no reason outside God Himself. The same verse begins with raq, 'yet' or 'only,' setting the whole of heaven and earth on one side and this small people on the other.

The command of verse 16 is literally 'circumcise the foreskin of your heart,' using orlah, the ordinary word for a foreskin. Hebrew applies the image of an uncircumcised organ to anything closed or unresponsive. Moses calls himself literally 'uncircumcised of lips' in Exodus 6:12, where the BSB has 'unskilled in speech,' and Jeremiah 6:10 says the people's ears are literally uncircumcised, rendered 'closed.' An uncircumcised heart is one covered over, unable to hear or respond. The parallel clause, 'stiffen your necks no more,' uses the same root qashah as the 'stiff-necked' of 9:6 and 9:13. Moses joins two images of resistance, a covered heart and a rigid neck.

The titles of verse 17 use a Hebrew superlative. 'God of gods and Lord of lords' is formed like 'Song of Songs' or 'the holy of holies': the supreme member of the class. The verse does not concede that other gods are real rivals; it says whatever claims to rule is ruled by Him. Then come three adjectives, great, mighty and awesome, the same triad Nehemiah prays in Nehemiah 9:32. 'Awesome' is nora, a form of yare, the very verb of 'fear' in verses 12 and 20. God is the One rightly feared; that is why Israel is told to fear Him.

His justice is described with two courtroom idioms. 'Showing no partiality' is literally 'He does not lift faces,' the gesture of a judge who raises the face of a favored petitioner. 'Accepting no bribe' uses shochad, the gift that Deuteronomy 16:19 says blinds the eyes of the wise. The God who could not be bought is the one who 'executes justice' for those who have nothing to offer, verse 18. Paul's 'God does not show favoritism,' Romans 2:11, and Peter's in Acts 10:34 carry the same idea into Greek.

Finally, verse 21 says 'He is your praise,' using tehillah. God is not only the One Israel praises; He is Israel's glory, the thing they boast in. Jeremiah prays the same words, 'You are my praise,' Jeremiah 17:14. And the footnote to verse 4 gives the Hebrew name for the Ten Commandments, literally 'the Ten Words,' which through the Greek became the English word Decalogue.

typology.type: The call to circumcise the heart, not merely the flesh
typology.fulfillment: Moses commands Israel to cut away the covering of their own hearts, yet the same book admits they cannot, promising instead that 'the LORD your God will circumcise your hearts,' Deuteronomy 30:6. Paul identifies that promised work with union with Christ: 'In Him you were also circumcised,' with 'the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11. True circumcision is 'a matter of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29. The escalation is from a command addressed to the stubborn to a gift worked in them. The sign on the flesh fell short because it could mark a body without changing a heart, Jeremiah 9:25-26.

typology.type: Levi, whose inheritance is the LORD Himself rather than land
typology.fulfillment: Levi received no territory, because 'the LORD is his inheritance,' verse 9. What was the particular portion of one tribe becomes the confession of every believer who can say, 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever,' Psalm 73:26. In Christ the priestly calling passes to the whole people of God, 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, whose inheritance is kept in heaven. The type falls short because Levi still depended on the other tribes' tithes to live; in Christ believers are 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17, possessing God Himself and, with Him, all things.

typology.type: The new tablets placed in the ark, the covenant kept in God's presence
typology.fulfillment: After the first tablets were broken, God wrote the same words again and had them kept inside the ark, where they 'remained,' verse 5, beneath the mercy seat, Hebrews 9:4-5. The law of God was guarded at the place where atonement was made. Christ is the One in whom God's law is perfectly kept, the One who delights to do God's will with His law within His heart, and He Himself is the place of atonement. The type falls short because tablets in a box could not enter the people; the new covenant writes God's laws 'on their hearts,' Hebrews 8:10.

typology.type: Israel, once foreigners in Egypt, commanded to love the foreigner
typology.fulfillment: Israel's memory of being foreigners in Egypt was to shape how they treated the ger among them, verse 19. The pattern reaches its height in the gospel. Gentiles were once 'strangers to the covenants of the promise,' Ephesians 2:12, and are now 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens,' Ephesians 2:19. Christ Himself identifies with the stranger, 'I was a stranger and you took Me in,' Matthew 25:35. The escalation is that God's love for the foreigner, shown in food and clothing, becomes adoption into His household through the blood of Christ.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the question of verse 12. Moses asks what God wants and answers with love, fear and wholehearted service. When a lawyer asked Jesus which commandment was greatest, He answered in Deuteronomy's terms, loving God with all the heart and soul and mind, Matthew 22:37-38. But Jesus did more than restate the demand; He was the one man who met it. Where Israel stiffened its neck, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, Philippians 2:8. When tempted to bow to another, He quoted the very words of verse 20, 'Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only,' Matthew 4:10. The requirement of Deuteronomy 10 is first fulfilled in the life of Jesus before it is ever produced in His people.

Second, the chapter leads to Christ through the heart. Moses commands a circumcision Israel cannot perform, and Deuteronomy 30:6 promises God will do it. The New Testament says this happens in Christ. Believers are circumcised 'in Him,' by a circumcision 'performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11, and Paul immediately links it to being buried and raised with Him in baptism. The inward change Moses called for is the new birth that Christ gives by His Spirit, so that the first and greatest commandment becomes, for the first time, a desire rather than only a demand. 'We love because He first loved us,' 1 John 4:19.

Third, there is the priesthood. Levi was set apart to carry the ark, to stand before the LORD and to bless in His name. Christ is the priest who does all three. He bears the covenant, since in Him the law is kept; He stands before the Father on our behalf; and He blesses. The last picture of Jesus in Luke's Gospel is of Him lifting His hands and blessing His disciples as He is carried into heaven. Levi's inheritance was the LORD; Christ's inheritance is the nations, and His people are heirs with Him.

Fourth, the God of verses 17 and 18 is seen in the face of Jesus. The God of gods who accepts no bribe and feeds the foreigner walks among the poor, eats with outsiders, and welcomes the Canaanite woman and the Samaritan. In Christ the 'great, mighty, and awesome God' draws near to the fatherless and the widow. At His return He bears the title of verse 17, 'KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS,' Revelation 19:16. The chapter guards against forced allegory at one point: the ark and tablets are not a coded picture of Christ in every detail. The link is theological. The covenant God renewed after the calf is the covenant He fulfils in His Son.
study.god:
Verse 14 sets the scale. To the LORD belong the heavens, even 'the highest heavens,' literally the heavens of the heavens, and the earth and everything in it. Solomon would later say that 'heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You,' 1 Kings 8:27. God needs nothing, owns everything, and is contained by nothing. That is the backdrop against which verse 15 lands with such force: 'Yet the LORD has set His affection on your fathers.' The chapter holds God's transcendence and His particular love side by side and refuses to let either diminish the other.

The chapter also shows God's constancy after sin. He writes the same words on the new tablets that He wrote on the first, verse 4. He does not lower the standard to accommodate Israel's failure, nor does He withdraw the covenant. Forgiveness in the Bible is never God pretending the law does not matter. It is God keeping both His law and His people.

Verses 17 and 18 contain one of the fullest descriptions of God in Deuteronomy. He is supreme over every power, 'God of gods and Lord of lords.' He is 'great, mighty, and awesome,' a God rightly feared. He is perfectly just, showing no partiality and taking no bribe. And that just God 'executes justice for the fatherless and widow' and 'loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing.' What is striking is the order. Immediately after His highest titles come His lowliest works. Psalm 113:5-7 marvels in the same way: the One enthroned on high 'raises the poor from the dust.' Isaiah 57:15 says the high and holy One dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit.' God's greatness is not shown in distance from the weak but in stooping to them.

This shapes worship and ethics together. Because God loves the foreigner, Israel must love the foreigner, verse 19. The command is not a separate social program attached to religion; it is the imitation of God. To neglect the outsider is to misrepresent the God one claims to worship, which is why the law later curses anyone 'who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow,' Deuteronomy 27:19, and why the prophets tie true worship to justice, Zechariah 7:9-10 and Malachi 3:5.

Finally, God is Israel's praise, verse 21. The God who made them 'as numerous as the stars' from seventy souls, verse 22, is the One they boast in. Worship that fits this chapter is reverent, since He is awesome, intimate, since He has set His affection on His people, and practical, since it spills over into love for those with no one else to defend them.

crossReferences.note: The original account of the second tablets. God tells Moses to chisel out two tablets 'like the originals' and promises to write the same words on them. Deuteronomy 10:1-5 retells it with the added detail of the ark, showing that the renewed covenant was a restoration of the first, not a new and lesser one.

When the ark entered Solomon's temple it held nothing but 'the two stone tablets that Moses had placed in it at Horeb.' The note in Deuteronomy 10:5, 'there they have remained,' was still true generations later, a quiet witness that God's covenant word had been kept among His people.

God tells Aaron, 'I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites.' Deuteronomy 10:9 applies the same grant to the whole tribe of Levi. The priests' lack of land was not deprivation but privilege, and it explains the book's repeated care for the Levite.

Micah asks what the worshiper should bring, thousands of rams or even a firstborn, and answers that the LORD requires justice, mercy and a humble walk with God. It is a prophetic summary built on the same logic as Deuteronomy 10:12-13, that God seeks the person, not merely the offering.

The command of 10:16 becomes a promise: 'The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts.' Deuteronomy itself anticipates that Israel will fail to do what 10:16 commands, and that God will one day do it for them, so that they may love Him with all their heart.

Jeremiah repeats Moses' command to Judah on the eve of exile, 'remove the foreskins of your hearts,' and warns of wrath like fire. The call of Deuteronomy 10:16 was still unanswered centuries later, which is why Jeremiah goes on to promise a new covenant written on the heart, 31:33.

Paul defines a true Jew as one who is so inwardly, with circumcision 'a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code.' He is developing Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6 directly, and adds that such a person's praise comes from God, echoing 'He is your praise' in 10:21.

Believers were 'circumcised' in Christ, 'with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands.' Paul names Christ as the one who does what Moses commanded and Deuteronomy 30:6 promised: the cutting away of the old, stubborn self.

Peter's words at Cornelius's house, 'God does not show favoritism,' apply Deuteronomy 10:17 to the inclusion of the Gentiles. The God who loves the foreigner and does not lift faces is the God who gives His Spirit to a Roman centurion's household.

The foreigner is to be treated 'as native-born' and loved 'as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.' Deuteronomy 10:19 gives the same command and the same reason, and adds that it is grounded in God's own love for the foreigner in verse 18.

The LORD enthroned on high 'raises the poor from the dust.' The psalm sings the pairing found in Deuteronomy 10:14-18, supreme majesty joined to care for the lowly, and turns the doctrine of this chapter into praise.

Jesus names wholehearted love for God as 'the first and greatest commandment.' His answer draws on Deuteronomy 6:5, and it gathers up the summary of 10:12, where fear, love, walking and serving are all expressions of one undivided devotion.

The rider on the white horse bears the name 'KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.' The title given to the LORD in Deuteronomy 10:17 belongs to the returning Christ, confirming that the God of gods of Moses' sermon is the God revealed in Jesus.

study.oneStory:
In the garden humanity was made to love and serve God freely, and the fall turned that love inward. By Deuteronomy 10 the story has shown that even a redeemed people carries the old heart with it: the calf at Horeb proved it. This chapter answers that disaster in two ways. God restores the covenant, writing His words again, and Moses names the real need, a heart that is circumcised and a neck that no longer stiffens.

The chapter also gathers up the promises to the patriarchs. Seventy went down to Egypt; now they are as numerous as the stars, verse 22, exactly as God told Abraham in Genesis 15:5. The God who owns the heavens has kept His word to one family, and He has done it with the whole world in view, for the love that chose Israel is the same love that feeds the foreigner.

What the chapter sets up is a long wait. Israel's history in the land shows the heart was not yet changed. The prophets saw it plainly: 'the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart,' Jeremiah 9:26. So they looked forward to a day when God Himself would give a new heart and put His Spirit within, Ezekiel 36:26-27, and write His law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33.

That day dawns in Christ. He fulfils the demand of verse 12 in His own life, and by His death and resurrection He performs the circumcision not made with hands, Colossians 2:11. The Spirit He pours out begins to produce in His people the love Moses asked for. The outsider is brought in; Gentiles who were strangers become fellow citizens, Ephesians 2:19. And the church becomes the priestly people whose inheritance is God Himself.

The story ends in the new creation, where the loving God who stooped to feed foreigners will gather people from every nation into one household. There no neck will stiffen and no heart will be closed. The first and greatest commandment will be kept, not by strain but by nature, because God will be His people's praise forever.

quiz.q: What did God instruct Moses to make in order to receive the new tablets (v.1)?

options.text: An ark of wood, alongside two new stone tablets like the first ones.
options.note: Verse 1 gives this exact instruction.

options.text: A golden calf to replace the broken idol.
options.note: The golden calf was the sin being judged, not something God commanded to be remade.

options.text: New clothing for the priests.
options.note: No such instruction appears in this passage.

options.text: Nothing new was to be made.
options.note: Verse 1 explicitly instructs Moses to make an ark and new tablets.

quiz.q: According to verse 8, what was the tribe of Levi specifically set apart to do?

options.text: Carry the ark of the covenant, stand before the LORD to serve Him, and pronounce blessings in His name.
options.note: Verse 8 lists these three specific duties given to Levi.

options.text: Farm the land on Israel's behalf.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly says Levi received no land inheritance at all, the opposite of this option.

options.text: Lead Israel's armies into battle.
options.note: No military role is described for Levi in this passage.

options.text: Nothing specific is mentioned about Levi's calling.
options.note: Verse 8 gives explicit detail about their calling.

quiz.q: According to verses 12-13, what does the LORD actually require of Israel?

options.text: To fear Him, walk in His ways, love Him, serve Him with all their heart and soul, and keep His commandments for their own good.
options.note: Verses 12-13 list exactly these requirements.

options.text: To offer as many sacrifices as possible regardless of the heart's condition.
options.note: The emphasis here is entirely on the heart's posture, not on the quantity of ritual sacrifice.

options.text: To build the largest and most impressive temple possible.
options.note: No temple-building requirement appears in this passage.

options.text: Nothing specific is required.
options.note: Verses 12-13 give a clear, specific summary of what is required.

quiz.q: What does Moses mean by commanding Israel to 'circumcise your hearts' (v.16)?

options.text: To remove the resistance and stubbornness of their inner life, not merely perform an external rite.
options.note: The phrase is paired with 'stiffen your necks no more,' pointing to an inward, not merely physical, transformation.

options.text: To undergo a repeated physical surgery.
options.note: The command is explicitly metaphorical, applied to the heart, not a repeated physical procedure.

options.text: To abandon the covenant sign of circumcision altogether.
options.note: The command intensifies, rather than abandons, the meaning behind the existing covenant sign.

options.text: Nothing about the heart is intended by this phrase.
options.note: The phrase explicitly names the heart as its object.

quiz.q: How does Moses describe God's care for the vulnerable in verses 18-19?

options.text: He executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner too, since they themselves were foreigners in Egypt.
options.note: Verses 18-19 state this directly, grounding the command in Israel's own history.

options.text: He ignores the vulnerable entirely, favoring only the powerful.
options.note: The text states the opposite, that God shows no partiality and specifically cares for the vulnerable.

options.text: He commands Israel to exploit foreigners for labor.
options.note: The command is to love the foreigner, the opposite of exploitation.

options.text: Nothing is said about the fatherless, widow, or foreigner.
options.note: Verses 18-19 speak of them explicitly.

questions: God's true requirement, according to Moses, is not empty ritual but a heart that fears, loves, and walks with Him. Where might your own faith have drifted into external motions without inner devotion?
'Circumcise your heart' calls for inward transformation, not just an outward sign. What stubborn resistance in your heart needs God's cutting, transforming work right now?

God cares for the fatherless, the widow, and the foreigner, and commands Israel to do the same because they themselves were once foreigners. Who is the vulnerable person God is calling you to love practically this week?
Levi's inheritance was the LORD Himself, not land or property. Is your own sense of security and identity rooted more in what you possess, or in the LORD Himself?
Even after the golden calf, God gave Moses new tablets and started again with His people. Where do you need to receive a fresh start from God rather than living under the weight of past failure?

translationNotes.note: 'Circumcise your hearts' is a metaphor drawn from the physical covenant sign, later developed by Jeremiah 4:4 and Paul in Romans 2:28-29 to describe an inward, Spirit-wrought transformation.
'God of gods and Lord of lords' is a Hebrew superlative construction expressing absolute supremacy, not an acknowledgment that other gods actually exist as rivals to Him.
The figure of seventy who went down to Egypt echoes the genealogical list in Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5, anchoring this chapter's praise of Israel's growth in specific, remembered history.
